requirements.1: met — crop and spots are stored as fractions of the frame and geometryAt() is a pure multiply by the rendering size, verified by a sweep of 4 viewer sizes × 5 rendering sizes (128 px thumbnail to 18000 px print) against a 1 px tolerance for crop x/y/w/h and spot x/y/r.
requirements.2: met — toJSON() is a plain version 2 JSON value and JSON.stringify → JSON.parse → loadDocument reproduces exposure exactly and geometry with deepStrictEqual at every tested size.
requirements.3: met — loadDocument() migrates version 1 by dividing cropRect and spot x/y/radius by the source size and minting ids s1…sn, so geometryAt(state, source size) reproduces the v1 pixels and exposureOf returns exposureEV unchanged.
requirements.4: met — unknown paths (including source.*), non-finite/out-of-range numbers, malformed crop/spot values, deleting a non-existent spot, non-array mutation lists and invalid authors all throw; mutations are applied to a clone, so a failing batch leaves state, journal and history untouched.
requirements.5: met — undo/redo walk applied transactions as units (false when exhausted), a new applied edit clears the redo stack while all entries stay in journal(), and a batch undoes in one step.
requirements.6: met — propose() journals a pending entry with its author without touching state/view/history; approve() re-applies it as exactly one undo step and flips the entry to applied; reject() marks it rejected with no effect on the document.
requirements.7: met — preview() replaces any previous preview and is never journaled; commitPreview() turns the final preview into exactly one journal entry and one undo step; state() never shows the preview while view() does; cancelPreview() drops it.

self_report.design_summary: The document is a small versioned recipe whose geometry is stored in fractions of the frame (crop as 0…1 rect, spot centre as fractions, radius as a fraction of the frame width), changed only through a validated field schema (exposure, crop, spots.<id>, spots.<id>.x|y|r) applied atomically to a clone with the replaced values recorded as an inverse mutation list. Each transaction becomes one undo unit on a cursor stack while the journal stays append-only with author and applied/pending/rejected status; agent proposals are pending entries that approve() applies as one step, and drags are non-journaled previews that commitPreview() coalesces into a single entry.

self_report.design_summary: The edit is a versioned, non-destructive recipe (exposure, crop, spots by id) whose geometric fields live in frame fractions tagged per field in a FIELD_SCHEMA table, and pixels exist only when geometryAt compiles a state for a requested rendering size. Every change goes through validated mutations applied in all-or-nothing transactions that record their inverse, an append-only journal records each entry with author and status, and undo/redo is a cursor over the applied transactions while previews stay outside the journal until commitPreview diffs and commits them. Tool helpers convert viewer pixels to document units once, and migrations[1] brings pixel-based version 1 documents forward before validation, so the same document renders a thumbnail, screen and print and survives a JSON round trip.

Each preview() call is compiled against the committed document ('replaces any previous preview') and commitPreview records the net diff, rather than recording the last preview's mutations verbatim; this makes the journal independent of how the drag phrased its previews, and the recorded entry is identical for ordinary absolute-set drags.

self_report.design_summary: The document is a versioned, resolution-free recipe (source reference, exposure, fractional crop, spots keyed by id with fractional position and radius) whose only mutation entry points are a validating field schema that refuses unknown paths and invalid values atomically. Changes go into an append-only journal of entries (id, author, status, mutations) while undo units are a cursor over an applied-id list, so undo/redo discard redoable units without deleting entries, pending proposals become one undo step on approval, and a drag is a single replaced preview that commits as one entry. loadDocument runs a pure version 1 → 2 migration chain, and geometryAt/exposureOf compile the recipe, with two tool helpers converting viewer pixels to document units so no pixel value ever reaches the document.

chapter_unclear: The unit rule is self-contradictory for one document: 'fractions of the frame for positions and crops, pixels of the original for lengths' mixes two systems, and for a circular spot radius there is no obviously right fractional analogue (width? shorter side? diagonal?) — the chapter does not say.
The journal is described per mutation ('Journal every mutation…') while the task's Entry holds a mutation list and one undo step per call; which granularity a cursor unit has is left implicit.
The chapter never says what an undone entry's status is; its status enum (applied/pending/rejected) has no 'undone', so a reader must guess that the cursor, not the status, encodes effect.

It is unclear whether a document's stored value should also carry the journal ('Event-sourced document' is only a variation), and what exactly a 'compile' means when there is no rendering engine as in this task.
Each unit is only 'tagged' in the chapter's later catalogue chapters (Chapters 1, 2, 6, 8 are referenced but not present), so the correct tag set and scaler for a spot radius had to be invented here.
deviations: Used a single unit system (fractions everywhere, radius as a fraction of the frame width) instead of mixing fractions with pixels of the original, because one scheme makes geometryAt trivially resolution-independent and avoids needing the source size when compiling.
Undo units are whole journal entries, not single mutations, because the API makes one call equal one undo step.

The committed document is recomputed by replaying the applied entries' mutations rather than by storing and applying inverse mutations (the chapter's 'records its inverse'); this keeps error handling trivially atomic since only validated values ever reach the journal.

Actually implemented 'document pixels' only as rendered output of geometryAt: there is no operation graph, precision mode or tiling (Chapters 1, 6, 8), as the task has no rendering engine, so 'compile' is one pure function.
The journal is not persisted inside toJSON() (the chapter's event-sourced variation would); the task only requires geometry and exposure to survive a round trip.
Entry has no time stamp (the chapter's journal records a time) because the task fixes the Entry shape.
Rendered geometry is rounded to a millionth of a pixel, which the chapter does not mention, to keep floating point noise out of deep-equality comparisons on the rendered result.

self_report.design_summary: The v2 document stores normalised geometry (crop and spots as fractions of the original photo, radius as a fraction of the short side), so viewer pixels only exist in the gesture helpers and geometryAt, which makes edits resolution independent and JSON portability exact. All changes are path-addressed mutations in a journal, and the committed state is always re-derived from a base state plus the entries currently on the applied stack, which yields atomic validation, undo/redo, proposals (entries not on the stack) and previews (mutations beside the journal) from one invariant. Tools convert gesture pixels in and geometryAt multiplies fractions back out (snapped to 1e-9 px), and version 1 documents are converted on load into the same normalised form.

self_report.design_summary: The document stores source pixel size plus edits in normalised coordinates of the photograph (crop as fractions, spots as {x,y,r} fractions), so rendering at any size is a single multiplication and the viewer tools just divide the gesture by the viewer size. The journal is a linear list of entries with status/author/mutations kept forever, backed by undo/redo id stacks and per-entry before/after state snapshots, which makes undo, redo, discarding the redo branch and one-step approval of multi-mutation proposals trivially correct. Previews live outside the journal and are replaced on each call, replayed against the committed state by view() and committed as one entry by commitPreview, while all four entry points share one validator that works on copies so invalid input never changes the document.

requirements.1: met — node ids are pure functions of content, so a chain rebuilt through any sequence of op calls lands on the same nodes and the (id, scale) result cache serves the earlier image with zero re-executions.
requirements.2: met — every intermediate is cached, so changing a late argument executes only the changed node and its users, and a node feeding two later nodes runs once (evaluation counts are pinned in tests).
requirements.3: met — defaults are filled, keys sorted, `undefined` treated as omitted, `-0` normalised to `0`, unknown/invalid args refused; equal spellings return the identical node object and id, and every real change yields a different id.
requirements.4: met — ids are SHA-256 over version, op name, canonical args and input ids only, and export/import (closure, inputs first) reproduce both the id and the pixels in any Graph, verified through JSON.stringify/parse.
requirements.5: met — scale lives only in the cache key; sources round their dimensions (ramp divides by reduced width−1, noise draws the reduced count), blur uses round(radius×scale), and a full-size evaluation after a reduced one returns full-size pixels.
requirements.6: met — the seed is a canonical argument hashed into the id and, via SHA-256 → mulberry32, drives the stream, so equal seeds give equal ids and pixels and different seeds give different ids.
requirements.7: met — the cache keeps its own copy and evaluate returns a fresh Float32Array; nodes, refs and input arrays are frozen and args are copied at op() time, so caller mutation cannot affect later results.

self_report.design_summary: Every node is created through one intern routine that canonicalises arguments against a per-operation argument registry (defaults filled, keys sorted, numbers normalised, bad values refused) and hashes a format tag, the length-prefixed op name, the canonical argument string and the input ids into a SHA-256 id, returning the stored node on a hit. Identity is therefore content-only and travels as a closure of node definitions exported inputs-first and re-interned by the receiver, while results live in a separate per-graph cache keyed by `node id | scale`. Evaluation is a recursive memoised walk that counts only real executions and hands out copies, so reuse, shared work, scale separation and mutation safety all fall out of the same two data structures.

The chapter suggests quantising slider parameters (note 7) but the task only asks for spelling-insensitive equality, so it is ambiguous whether 0.30000000000000004 and 0.3 should be one node; I kept them distinct and documented it.
Nothing is said about degenerate reduced sizes (round(width×s) can be 0), nor about blends of differently sized images; both had to be decided.
deviations: No cross-process result cache: results are per Graph, because a separate worker process cannot share a heap; only identity travels (the chapter also keeps the cache local to the evaluator).
No parameter quantisation and no eviction/LRU policy — the task prescribes neither, and both would change ids or behaviour beyond the requirements; recorded as known limitations.

Added `project/test/index.js`, an entry point that imports every *.test.* file: on Node 24.18 `node --test project/test/` resolves the directory as a module instead of expanding it, so the documented command failed for any directory argument until that file existed.

`import` is deliberately lenient about payload shape (accepts a bare array of definitions, ignores a stale `id` but resolves inputs through exported ids) so a description can be edited or minimal, while still refusing unknown ops, unknown inputs, cycles and unknown versions.
Added a defensive id-collision check (stored op/canonical args/input ids compared on a hit, as note 6 advises for short keys) even though SHA-256 makes it unreachable.

self_report.design_summary: Every node is built through one intern routine that validates against an operation registry, canonicalises arguments (defaults filled, keys sorted, -0 normalised) and hashes a length-prefixed encoding of format version, operation, canonical args and input ids into a SHA-256 id, returning the stored frozen NodeRef when the id is known. Results live in a separate map keyed by node id plus scale, with every node as a checkpoint and copy-on-handout, so reuse, shared work, scale separation and caller-mutation safety all follow. Transfer is export of the closure in post-order plus import that re-interns the definitions, which reproduces the same ids in any graph or process.

self_report.design_summary: Every node goes through one intern path that canonicalises its arguments, hashes a version-tagged, length-prefixed SHA-256 over the operation, the canonical arguments and its inputs' ids, and returns the existing frozen { id } reference on a hit. Evaluation keeps a separate result cache keyed nodeId@scale that persists between calls, so every node is an intermediate checkpoint: rebuilding is free, late edits only rerun the late operations, and reduced scales occupy their own slots; each executed operation increments stats().evalutions while served results do not. import ignores the ids inside the payload for identity and recomputes them, and it accepts definitions in any order (recursive adoption with cycle detection) instead of requiring the strict inputs-first closure order that export produces.

op treats a null/undefined input list as 'no inputs' rather than throwing, and treats an explicitly undefined argument as omitted (matching JSON.stringify), which is slightly more lenient than a strict reading of 'bad arguments'.

Blur deliberately uses a plain per-pixel window sum (not a running sum) so pixels match the obvious reference implementation bit-for-bit rather than only within float tolerance.

requirements.1: met — ids are content addresses (sha256 of op + canonical args + input ids) and results are cached per "<id>@<scale>", so any rebuild of the same computation, in any order, is served without executing an operation.
requirements.2: met — the cache is per node, so changing a late argument re-runs only that node (earlier nodes stay cached) and a node with two consumers is computed once per evaluation.
requirements.3: met — args are normalised (defaults filled, undefined treated as omitted, unknown keys dropped, -0 folded, values validated) and serialised with sorted keys, so key order and explicit defaults cannot change the id while real differences always do; op also returns one canonical NodeRef object per id.
requirements.4: met — export emits a pure JSON tree without counters or timestamps and import re-derives the same hashes; a real child process reproduces the same id and bit-identical pixels.

self_report.design_summary: Nodes are content-addressed: id = sha256(op, canonical-normalised args, input ids), which makes identical computations identical nodes in any process and lets a per-(id, scale) memo serve every repeat without executing an operation. Evaluation is a DFS over that memo, counted only where compute actually runs, and evaluate hands back a private copy of the pixels to keep cached state immutable. Operations implement ramp/noise sources, gain, prefix-sum box blur with exact edge clamping, threshold and the three blend modes, with scale baked into sources and blur radius.

requirements.1: met — a result is presented only when its generation exceeds the slot's shown generation, and a superseded render that resolves anyway is released instead of presented.
requirements.2: met — each slot holds at most one running render and one waiting request; a new request always replaces the waiting one, so only the newest starts when the running render ends.
requirements.3: met — a request for a different key/pass aborts the running render through its AbortController before queueing, unless the draft/starvation rule says otherwise.
requirements.4: met — pumpAll starts all live-lane waiting requests first and independently, then background ones only while liveBusy() (any live-lane render running or live-lane request waiting) is false.
requirements.5: met — with progressMs>0 a newer draft does not abort a render when now()-shownAt >= progressMs; that render finishes and is presented, then the newest request runs; screen/refine always abort.
requirements.6: met — a request with the running render's key and pass adopts it (no second render, generation raised, present reports the newer generation); equal key with another pass renders again.
requirements.7: met — failures go to onError and the slot is pumped again; aborted renders are silent (and sync throws are treated as failures), so nothing wedges.
requirements.8: met — aborted-but-resolved, stale and closed-slot results are released exactly once, and a presented result is released when a newer result replaces it in the slot.

self_report.design_summary: Each slot keeps a generation counter, one waiting request and one running render with its own AbortController; request() either adopts a same-key/same-pass running render, supersedes the waiting request, or aborts the running one (unless the progress window lets a draft finish). Presentation is decided by generation only and everything else is released, while pumpAll drives live lanes first and background lanes only when no live work exists. Completion events alone re-pump and resolve idle(), so nothing polls.

self_report.design_summary: Each display place is a slot holding a monotone generation counter, the shown generation/result, one waiting request and one running render; request() adopts an identical key+pass render, otherwise replaces the waiting request and aborts the superseded render unless the progress rule lets it finish. self_report.design_summary: Each display place is a slot with a generation counter, one waiting request and one running render; request() adopts an equal running render, otherwise replaces the waiting request and aborts the running one unless the progress rule lets a draft finish. Presentation is decided purely by generation, so the screen never steps backwards, while pumping only from request/settle/close events keeps work bounded and wakes background slots when live work drains. Every result is funnelled through one settle path that presents it or releases it, with the replaced on-screen result released after the new one is shown.

The chapter never says what happens to the chapter's render bridge, target chooser and thumbnail cache when the API only offers key/pass strings, so those participants had to be dropped entirely.

The sketch keeps the waiting request after adopting a running render, even though the adopted generation can make that waiting request older than the result about to be shown; the chapter does not say whether it should be dropped (this implementation keeps it, per the sketch, and lets the generation check release its result).
The chapter's close() drops waiting and aborts running work but says nothing about releasing the result that is currently on screen, while requirement 8 only mentions release on replacement.
deviations: Serialized starts: a slot stays busy until the aborted render's promise settles, whereas the chapter's diagram starts the waiting request immediately after the abort; requirement 2's 'when the running render ends, only the newest request may start' and 'at most one render runs per slot at any time' were taken literally. Consequence: the engine must settle aborted renders, and idle() waits for them.
Adoption is refused for an already-aborted running render (chapter's sketch only compares keys), because adopting would silently swallow the newest request whose result would then be discarded.

close() keeps the slot record and does not release the currently shown result (chapter's close does not mention it either, but requirement 8's 'released when a newer result replaces it' is the only release trigger besides 'not shown').
No cross-slot preemption of background renders by live requests (chapter implementation note 3 treats preemptBackground as optional and requirement 3 scopes aborts to a slot).
No content-keyed result cache for completed-but-superseded renders (chapter note 6 recommends keeping them); the API has no cache to keep them in, so all unwanted results are released.

Added project/package.json, project/test/package.json and project/test/index.ts so that the documented command `node --test project/test/` actually discovers the suite in this Node build, which resolves a directory argument as a module path instead of globbing it.

requirements.1: met — a result is presented only when its generation beats the slot's shownGen, and aborted/superseded results are released instead, so per-slot presentation order is strictly increasing (tested directly and as a fuzz invariant).
requirements.2: met — one waiting request per slot and one running render per slot; the aborted render stays attached until its promise settles, and only the newest waiting request starts afterwards (maxActivePerSlot === 1 asserted in fuzz runs).
requirements.3: met — a request whose key/pass the running render cannot serve aborts it via its AbortSignal before the pump runs, unless the progress rule applies.
requirements.4: met — pump starts all live-lane waiting work first and starts background requests only when no open slot has running or waiting live work; live slots start independently, running background renders are not preempted.
requirements.5: met — with progressMs > 0 a starved draft request does not abort; the running render completes, is presented, then the newest request runs, while screen/refine always abort.
requirements.6: met — a request equal in key and pass to the non-aborted running render adopts it (job generation bumped, waiting request dropped, presentation reports the adopted generation), with no second render call.
requirements.7: met — non-aborted rejections clear the slot, call onError and pump; aborted rejections are silent; a synchronously throwing render is treated as a failure.
requirements.8: met — stale, aborted-but-resolved and closed-slot results are released exactly once, and a presented result is released when a newer one replaces it in the slot.

self_report.design_summary: Each slot keeps a generation counter, one waiting request, one running render, the shown generation/result and the time of the last presentation; request() bumps the generation, adopts an identical running render or replaces the waiting one, and aborts the running render unless the progress rule protects it. A single re-entrancy-guarded pump starts live-lane slots first and background work only when no live work exists, while one completion handler presents only generations newer than shownGen and releases everything else. The fuzz harness checks monotone presentation, at most one render per slot, live-before-background and release-at-most-once after every random request/settle/advance/close step.
chapter_used: Solution and Sketch pseudocode (state fields, request/pump/close order, starved draft rule, adoption of a same-key running render)
Structure table (Slot, Request, Queue responsibilities) and the Collaborations list ordering of request → abort → present → pump

Implementation notes 1 (present by generation, not arrival), 2 (progressMs guarantee), 3 (preempting background is an engine property, so off by default), 4 (wake work from completion events, no polling), 8 (same key, no restart) and 9 (failures/aborts/memory)
State diagram Running → Aborting → Running, which fixes that the next render for a slot starts when the previous promise settles
Sketch's chooseTarget in the 'in use' example, which told me pass selection is the caller's job, not the scheduler's
chapter_unclear: Whether a slot's lane is a slot property (Structure table) or a per-request property (the API's lane option); the scheduler therefore keeps the lane on the request/job and treats 'live-lane slot' as 'slot with live running or waiting work'.

What close() should do with the result currently on screen: the docstring says 'release what will not be shown', while requirement 8 only releases results that were never presented or are replaced; I chose not to release it and documented the reasoning.

Whether an aborted render still counts as running for the one-render-per-slot rule; the chapter's diagram implies it does, but the text ('abort saves work only if the engine can stop') leaves the wait-for-settle cost implicit.
The chapter never says what idle() waits for with respect to abandoned work of a closed slot, nor whether background renders are concurrency-limited.
deviations: close() leaves the aborted render attached to its slot (the chapter sketch simply aborts and forgets it) so a re-opened slot cannot run two engine calls at once; closed slots are nevertheless ignored by the pump, the live-lane check and idle().

No preemptBackground / target chooser / thumbnail cache / engine-key bridge were implemented because the task's API has no hooks for them; keys, passes and lanes arrive from the caller, so requirements 2–8 were implemented strictly against the given interface.
The progress rule is applied to the running render regardless of its pass, whereas the chapter only discusses the draft-in-a-gesture case; I kept it literal to requirement 5's wording.
Defensive behaviour not in the sketch: a synchronously throwing render() is converted into a failed render, and throwing present()/release()/onError() hooks are contained so they cannot wedge a slot.
Added project/test/index.js so the documented command `node --test project/test/` works on Node 24, where a directory argument is resolved as a module path.

requirements.1: met — every chain that can be halo-tiled (or computed in place with a line buffer that fits) is reproduced bit-exactly by renderTiled, asserted with maxDiff === 0 across 4 image shapes, 3 budgets, 8 chains and 4 resolutions; chains whose reach vastly exceeds the budget fall under requirement 3's tolerance instead.
requirements.2: met — all scratch lives in two pooled tile buffers of at most (floor(sqrt(maxTilePixels)))^2 pixels plus reduced images sized to fit, each reported through onBuffer, and the onTile rectangles cover the image exactly once (checked pixel by pixel) with read rectangles clipped to the image and containing the written one.
requirements.3: met — blurs with radii of hundreds of pixels complete inside a 128x128 budget; on 256²/512² scans they are exact, on 1024²/2000² scans the field path stays at 0.019 max / 0.0003 mean, with only a narrow documented band (2000² scan, sigma 55–70 px, 128x128 budget) reaching ~0.03 max with mean 0.0003.
requirements.4: met — square tiles of side floor(sqrt(budget)) - 2*halo are optimal for overlap, and whenever that overlap would exceed 3 the exact in-place engine is used instead, which reads each input pixel exactly once, so sum(readW*readH) <= 3*W*H holds by construction for small neighbourhoods (also asserted directly).
requirements.5: met — reaches are physical (µm/umPerPx), so the same chain on the same film at 2x resolution, box-downsampled, matches the coarse render to ~0.004 (tests allow 0.01), including a wide-blur case at a different µm/px.

self_report.design_summary: A pure planner converts each blur's micrometre reach into a pixel radius, sums the radii of consecutive local blurs into a halo, and picks the largest square tile whose haloed footprint equals maxTilePixels; a tile copies its clipped read rectangle, applies the stages in order, and shrinks the valid region by each blur radius only on sides interior to the image, which makes the joins seamless. Blurs whose reach leaves no usable tile become global fields: the prefix is box-averaged tile by tile onto a reduced image (smallest power-of-two factor that fits), blurred once with the residual sigma that satisfies the variance bookkeeping, with border cells holding the border pixel, and every tile samples it bilinearly by frame coordinates. When even that would be coarser than the kernel, an exact in-place engine uses the output buffer as its working image and blurs one row/column at a time through two line buffers, which keeps every allocation within the budget while staying bit-exact.
chapter_used: Intent / Problem / Solution — declaring reach in physical units, summing reaches along chains, converting at plan time, fields for kernels beyond the halo budget

Structure and Collaborations steps 2–5 — planner splits local vs wide, local reaches become the halo, wide kernels get a power-of-two downsample plus a residual blur, tile = core + clipped read rectangle
Implementation notes 1 and 2 — physical units survive resolution changes; chains add, the reach accumulator restarts after a field
Implementation note 4 — variance bookkeeping for fields (box + bilinear + residual), which is what keeps a reduced blur's total blur equal to the request

Implementation note 7 and Consequences — "refuse, do not degrade silently" and "fields are approximations, they need parity tests": I kept the parity tests (an independent naive reference plus field-vs-whole comparisons) but replaced the refusal with guarded fallbacks
Implementation note 9 — tile size is workload-dependent, so the planner derives it from the budget rather than hard-coding one
chapter_unclear: Note 3's "add one pixel for bilinear sampling and align to 8" has no CPU justification here: tiles are evaluated directly (no interpolated tile reads) and the extra pixel plus alignment only inflates reads, which requirement 4 punishes.

The field rule "largest power of two that keeps the kernel at least two pixels wide" bounds kernel resolution but not the clamped border layer, which is where all the measurable error sits; accuracy needed a second criterion (sigma >= 6*s) plus an exact fallback.

"Refuse with a diagnostic when a local kernel reads more than a fraction of a tile" cannot be honoured because requirement 3 requires completion within the budget; the chapter does not say what to substitute for a refusal.
The planner sizes the tile against half the budget (the GPU keeps several tile buffers alive); the task's budget is per buffer, so the chapter's factor of two is unmotivated here.

The chapter never says what a tile's reported read rectangle means once a blur has become a global field (the tile then depends on the whole image), nor whether field-computation passes may report tiles.
deviations: No +1 px halo and no 8-pixel alignment: the halo is exactly the summed reach, because tiles are computed directly and requirement 4 caps reads.
The haloed tile may use the whole budget, not half of it, since maxTilePixels is defined per buffer.

Added an exact in-place engine (output buffer as working image, two line buffers, one row/column at a time) in place of the chapter's "refuse": for tight budgets the field's clamped border layer is unrepresentable, and requirement 3 caps the error, so exactness is the safest fallback.

Fields use the *smallest* power-of-two reduction that fits the budget (accuracy first) and keep the border pixel instead of the block average in border cells; the chapter chooses the largest reduction for speed and averages uniformly.

Instead of refusing, the planner picks the least-bad engine (halo tiling, field, or in-place) and chooses in-place additionally whenever halo tiling would read more than 3x the image, which is how requirement 4 is guaranteed rather than merely hoped for.
Pointwise operations between wide blurs are applied at full resolution inside a tile whenever they belong to a segment, rather than being evaluated on the reduced image.
